reference.source: Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: A movement disorder of involuntary, unilateral, irregular twitching of muscles innervated by the facial nerve, usually beginning around the eye and spreading over time to the lower face
It is typically unilateral and, unlike many other facial movement disorders, can persist during sleep
The most common cause is vascular compression of the facial nerve at its root exit zone from the brainstem, often by an ectatic or aberrant artery
Secondary causes include tumours, vascular malformations, and demyelinating or other lesions affecting the facial nerve pathway, which imaging helps exclude
Contraction of the frontalis and platysma together, or elevation of the eyebrow with eye closure (the 'other Babinski' sign), supports the diagnosis
It should be distinguished from blepharospasm, which is bilateral and involves only eye closure, and from facial myokymia and tics
MRI, often with vascular sequences, is used to evaluate for a compressive vessel or structural lesion along the nerve
Treatment principles include botulinum toxin injections as first-line symptomatic therapy and microvascular decompression surgery for suitable candidates seeking a durable cure
reference.pathophysiology: Hemifacial spasm is usually caused by pulsatile compression of the facial nerve at its root exit zone from the brainstem, most often by an aberrant or ectatic blood vessel. Chronic compression is thought to cause focal demyelination and ephaptic (cross) transmission between nerve fibres, together with hyperexcitability of the facial motor nucleus, generating spontaneous and spreading involuntary contractions. Secondary cases result from any lesion irritating the nerve along its course, and the pathophysiological common pathway is abnormal facial nerve excitability.
additionalDifferentials: Facial tics and functional facial movements
Partial motor seizures involving the face
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI with attention to the facial nerve root and vascular structures
Electrophysiological testing showing lateral spread response where diagnosis is uncertain
Evaluation for secondary structural or demyelinating causes when features are atypical
Clinical assessment to differentiate from blepharospasm and synkinesis
redFlags: Additional cranial nerve deficits or other neurological signs suggesting a structural posterior fossa lesion
Rapid progression or bilateral involvement warranting reassessment
Facial weakness or sensory change accompanying the spasm
Features suggesting a tumour or vascular malformation on imaging
reference.prognosis: Hemifacial spasm is typically chronic and does not resolve spontaneously, but it is not life-threatening; symptoms are well controlled with repeated botulinum toxin injections, and microvascular decompression offers a lasting cure in appropriately selected patients.
pitfalls: Confusing it with bilateral blepharospasm and choosing the wrong treatment approach
Failing to image for a compressive vessel or secondary lesion
Overlooking the diagnostic clue that spasms may persist during sleep
Not recognising post-palsy synkinesis, which can mimic hemifacial spasm
management: First-line symptomatic control with repeated botulinum toxin injections into the affected facial muscles, which are effective and well tolerated
Offer microvascular decompression of the facial nerve root exit zone as a potentially curative procedure in appropriately selected, fit patients
Trial oral agents such as carbamazepine, baclofen or clonazepam where injections are declined or as an adjunct, though these are less effective
Image with MRI focused on the facial nerve and vascular structures to identify the offending vessel and exclude a secondary tumour or demyelinating lesion
Distinguish from blepharospasm, facial myokymia and tics, using electrophysiology showing the lateral-spread response where the diagnosis is uncertain
Refer to neurology and neurosurgery, and reassure the patient that the condition, though chronic, is not life-threatening
